items.title: John Batiste "Bat" Stecklet Interview, 1959-06-15
items.q: But he was, he's the first man Al Hoyt blow jazz. And I'm willing to better all that, he was the foundation of jazz music. Because you take them nightclubs, like Al Hoyt and them fellas playing up in Boy Born Street there.

ctx.x: Did you ever play any more or less things like popular music of today? That is, it would sound anything more ragtime, you might say. Did you play much ragtime in your dance?

No, no. In our time, they never played that. The only man, like I told you before, that I heard putting the police band, got this fellow, Yellow Nunez, and I tell you, he couldn't read nothing, but he could, the minute he'd hear a piece, he could play it as good as you, you would notice. He had a good air. So the fire department, at least the police department, heard of Yellow Nunez, and the first thing you know, he had a uniform on, the police would have been a police band, Yellow Nunez. But he was, he's the…

stuff that they put in. It's not written. Now you said, you told me the other day that you played straight, but you played straight lead, but when the guys that you played with would sort of take off. Is that what you told me the other day? What's that about? You played, you said that you played the straight melody. Yeah, all the time. Right? But the guys that you were playing with might take off or play extra things.
